# On Dust

There is an hour, in late afternoon, when the sun clears the roof of the building across the street and comes into my apartment at a low angle, and everything I have failed to clean announces itself at once. The air turns into an aquarium. Motes wheel through the beam in slow spirals, rising on the warm current from the radiator, sinking as they cool, and the windowsill shows its grey felt like a confession. Here is the part I forget every winter and relearn every spring: the beam is visible only because of the dust. Pure air would give the light nothing to grip. What I am looking at is sunlight striking particles and scattering toward my eye — physicists call it the Tyndall effect; cathedral builders and cinematographers call it everything. Without dust, a sunbeam would be as invisible as gravity. Dust is the collaborator that lets us watch light travel.

I had meant to wipe the sill. Instead I knelt down and read it. Under the beam it resolves into an inventory: a nap of fibers — cotton, wool, one defiantly synthetic blue that used to be a sock or a blanket or a car seat; a sprinkle of sand; pollen in fine scales; soot that drifted in from the highway two blocks over; a flake of paint chipped off a window frame somebody painted badly years before I moved in; the hinge of an insect's wing; salt, from somewhere, from something that was once wet. None of it announces its origin. All of it testifies.

A French criminologist named Edmond Locard, working out of two attic rooms in Lyon in the first years of the last century, proposed what is now called the exchange principle: every contact leaves a trace. Touch anything and you carry something of it away on your hands and leave something of yourself behind. Forensic science is built on the idea. The windowsill is the principle made domestic. Nothing that enters a room entirely leaves it. It sheds; it mulches; it accedes.

Ask anyone what household dust is made of and they will say, with total confidence, dead skin. It mostly isn't. Analyses keep turning up the same roster: soil tracked in on shoes, textile fibers, soot, pollen, fragments of outdoor life of every provenance. Skin cells contribute a modest share, not the majority. The myth survives, I suspect, because it flatters us — we prefer to assume that even the dirt is about us, that the room fills with shed versions of ourselves. We do shed constantly, hundreds of millions of cells a day, a microscopic dandruff of the whole body. But most of it gets eaten, swept, vented. The dust is the world's. Even our errors about it are autobiographical.

What is genuinely new in dust is plastic. Every load of laundry releases fibers small enough to go airborne, and now they are in the rain and the snow and the sill — found, in recent years, in Alpine snowfields and Arctic ice, delivered by nothing but wind. The age of the molecule is also, it turns out, the age of the particle. My future archaeologists will be busy.

Plenty of what we shed doesn't get far. In the carpet, the mattress, the seam of the sofa live dermatophagoides — the name means skin-eater — mites the size of a punctuation mark that graze on our leavings and have kept us company so long that nobody remembers the terms of the arrangement. They are harmless unless you are allergic to them, in which case they are, statistically, among the most consequential animals you will ever host. We did not domesticate them. They domesticated us, or at least our real estate.

More intimate still are the Demodex mites that live in the follicles of nearly every adult human face — microscopic, worm-shaped, with mouthparts built for oil and, as far as anyone has been able to determine, no anus, so that everything they take in stays with them until they die. This is either a tragedy or a relief, depending on how you think about your own affairs. They emerge at night and crawl, at a stately pace, to the follicle next door to mate. Genetic studies suggest they inbreed cheerfully, have lost genes they no longer need, and may be drifting from parasites toward symbionts — or toward extinction; the biologists are split. Either way, our faces are their only continent. They go where we go.

Now the part I like best, the part that keeps me kneeling: not everything on the sill is from around here. The Earth accumulates space dust continuously. Most of it arrives as micrometeorites — grains smaller than a sand crystal that survive the plunge through air — and estimates of the annual harvest vary, but one recent count, based on Antarctic snow, put it around five thousand tons a year; older estimates ran several times that. Either way it is thousands of tons of extraterrestrial material settling onto the planet annually, a cosmic snowfall so steady and so fine that no one feels it land.

Jon Larsen, a Norwegian jazz guitarist with a geologist's habit of looking closely at things, noticed a strange bead on a picnic table one day — black, round, faintly metallic — and became obsessed with a question: could ordinary people find micrometeorites in ordinary places? He spent years collecting from rooftops and gutters, learned to distinguish cosmic spherules from industrial slag, consulted mineralogists, built a search protocol, and eventually published a photographic atlas of stardust found in cities. It turns out you can do this yourself. A magnet, a gutter, a microscope, patience. The beads are unmistakable once you know them: perfect little planets, glassy, sometimes holding chondrules that condensed before the planets did. Some of what falls is older than the ground it lands on.

So the oldest thing in my apartment is not the building, which dates from the 1920s and shows it. It is probably on the windowsill at this moment — a speck of grit, four and a half billion years old, waiting under the pollen for someone with a magnet and an afternoon.

Dust also has passports. Every year the winds lift something like a hundred and eighty million tons off the Sahara, and satellites with laser rangefinders have watched the plume cross the entire Atlantic and descend on the Amazon: tens of millions of tons annually, carrying on the order of twenty thousand tons of phosphorus. This is not a curiosity; it is a subsidy. Rain and rivers leach phosphorus out of the rainforest soil, and the dust arrives with almost exactly enough to replace it. The largest forest on Earth is partly dusted into existence by the largest desert on Earth — an arrangement between two extremes that neither could keep alone. Distance, at the scale of a particle, is a rumor.

The plume makes cameo appearances everywhere. West Africans know it as the harmattan, the dry season's veil. It falls as so-called blood rain on parked cars in England. It burnishes Florida's sunsets to an indecency. I look at the single grain of sand on my sill — beach sand, I had assumed, tracked in on somebody's shoe — and reconsider. The Atlantic is a thoroughfare. Grains commute.

And dust is not only freight; it is infrastructure. Nearly every raindrop condenses around a particle of something — salt, soot, mineral, spore — a nucleus for water to gather on. It never rains on nothing. The same is true of clouds generally, and of the climate itself, since airborne dust scatters sunlight, seeds clouds, and delivers iron to the open ocean, where plankton bloom in its wake. Remove the particulate and the sky stops working. The sky is mostly dust behaving well.

Because it falls everywhere, always, dust also becomes a record. Ice cores are banded with it; the layers read like tree rings, and a spike in ancient ice can mean an eruption on the far side of the world or a cold, dry age when the wind did more of the planet's bookkeeping. Loess — windblown silt — has stacked itself into cliffs hundreds of meters thick on the Chinese plateau, into the rolling hills of the Palouse. The history of the atmosphere is written in wind-laid flour. The planet keeps receipts. My windowsill, at modest scale, is doing what the glaciers do.

Ash is dust's heavy-handed older brother, and it, too, preserves. When Vesuvius buried Pompeii in the year 79, the bodies decayed inside the hardened ash and left voids — and in the 1860s an archaeologist named Giuseppe Fiorelli had the idea of pouring plaster into the cavities, recovering the shapes of the dead: a man shielding his face, a dog caught mid-struggle. At Herculaneum they found loaves of bread carbonized in an oven, mid-bake, the afternoon interrupted and then kept. Ash held the outline of a day.

Rooms do the same thing more slowly. Anyone who has moved a lamp that stood nine years in one corner knows the negative silhouette it leaves behind — a clean lamp-shape cut into the grey, a ghost made of absence. Take down a picture and the wall keeps its rectangle, dust-free, a framed nothing. A room remembers by what it protected from settling and for how long. Dust does not remember anything, strictly speaking. It indexes.

Whether dust is treasure or catastrophe is mostly a question of custody. In Victorian London, the heaps of cinders and rags and bone that dustmen carted away were valuable enough to found fortunes on. Dickens built a whole character around the fact: Noddy Boffin, the Golden Dustman of *Our Mutual Friend*, heir to a dust-heap empire. The ash went into bricks, the rags into paper, the bones into fertilizer, and coins and odd valuables sifted out along the way. The city's waste compounded like interest.

Seventy years later, American topsoil made the opposite journey. Farmers stripped the Plains of their grass, drought came, and soil that had taken centuries to build — an inch can take hundreds of years — went airborne in a handful of seasons. On Black Sunday, April 14, 1935, a wall of dirt rolled across the panhandles and turned afternoon into night. A wire-service reporter coined the phrase Dust Bowl the next morning and it stuck, the way everything out there stuck. There was such a thing as dust pneumonia; the lungs of children filled with their own state. Millions of people left the Plains during those years, refugees of their own ground, ground to powder. Same material, opposite entries: in London the dust was a fortune; in Oklahoma it was a debt called in. Dust is a ledger, and the handwriting is ours.

The moon, which has no wind and no rain, keeps its dust the way a miser keeps coins: forever, and in poor condition. With no weather to round the grains off, lunar dust stays sharp — jagged, interlocking, clingy with static. The Apollo astronauts found it stuck to everything, and when they came back inside and pulled their helmets off, they smelled it on their suits: spent gunpowder, several of them said. Harrison Schmitt came down with something the crews called lunar hay fever. It is the only place I know of where a footprint is a geological feature; the astronauts' bootprints could persist for millions of years before the slow rain of micrometeorites erases them. Earth reworks its dust endlessly. The moon merely annotates its own.

Mars is worse. There the dust is fine as talc and rust-red, and it goes global: in 2018 a planet-wide storm blotted the sun for weeks and months, and Opportunity — a rover built for ninety days that had already run fifteen years — starved in the dark, its solar panels

The request is open-ended: write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words. This is a creative freedom prompt. Let me think about what would make a compelling, substantial piece of writing.

Options:
1. A personal essay/meditation on some theme (time, memory, attention, cities, language)
2. A short story
3. A hybrid — an essayistic meditation with narrative elements
4. Something more experimental

Given "write freely," I think the best approach is something that genuinely feels like free writing but crafted — an essay that wanders but has a spine. A meditation on a subject that allows for texture, specificity, digression, and genuine thinking on the page. Subjects I could choose:

- The phenomenology of waiting rooms
- Night shifts and those who work them
- The history and feel of a particular sound (like the dial tone, or church bells)
- Attention and what it means to look at something for a long time
- Rivers, water infrastructure, the hidden city
- Letters, correspondence, the postal system
- The sea, lighthouses
- Insomnia and 3am consciousness
- The lost art of doing nothing
- Libraries and what they preserve
- Time capsules
- Shadows
- Dust — what dust actually is (skin cells, meteorite fragments, fabric fibers) — this is rich
- Empty buildings, abandoned malls
- The moon and how it's drifting away

I like the idea of writing about something small and overlooked that opens into something vast. Dust is great: it's cosmological (meteoritic dust settling on everything), biological (we are constantly shedding), architectural (dust as the record of a room's life), historical (dust of Pompeii, dust to dust), domestic (the dust on the windowsill as a slow clock). There's a wonderful fact that a significant amount of household dust is extraterrestrial — tens of thousands of tons of micrometeorites fall on Earth yearly. Also that dust from the Sahara crosses the Atlantic and fertilizes the Amazon. Dust as connection — everything connected through particles.

Alternatively, "night" — what happens at 3am, the people awake, the history of sleep (segmented sleep, "first sleep and second sleep" — Roger Ekirch's research). That's also rich.

Or attention: looking at a painting for three hours (there's a famous account of someone doing that at the Met with a Vermeer or the guy who spent 45 minutes... actually there's the practice of slow looking). 

Or the moon: it recedes 3.8 cm per year; moonlight is borrowed sunlight; the moon stabilizes Earth's axial tilt; "moonlight is 400,000 times dimmer than sunlight" etc.

Let me consider what I can sustain for ~2500 words with genuine interest and quality prose. A meditation on dust, structured as a wandering essay — starting with the dust on a windowsill, moving outward: what dust is made of, the cosmic origin of some of it, Sahara-to-Amazon dust, Pompeii, dust in literature (Dickinson's "I'm Nobody" — no, better: the phrase "as blind as..." no; "dust thou art"; the Dust Bowl; Middlemarch's "roar which lies on the other side of silence" — hmm that's about unregarded life), household archaeology, mites, the fact that dust holds the shape of rooms and lives (forensics — luminol, dust prints of removed objects — actually there's a real phenomenon: when an object sits somewhere for years and is removed, the dust pattern reveals its "shadow" — negative space ghosts). That's a beautiful image: the ghost of an absent object written in dust. Also conservation science: dust as data; ice cores; lakebed sediments.

Also "dust to dust" — mortality. And the Oostvaardersplassen — no, that's unrelated. Keep focused.
